learning_goal: Describe the femur as a whole bone — shaft, linea aspera, the two ends — name what attaches along it, explain why the shaft is a hollow tube with a medullary cavity rather than a solid rod, and predict the deformity, the blood loss and the compartment at risk in a fractured shaft.

structures.name: right femur
structures.label: Femur
structures.narration: The longest and strongest bone in the body. Take it as three pieces: an upper end that belongs to the hip, a shaft, and a lower end that belongs to the knee. The shaft is not straight — it is bowed forwards and it slants inwards from hip to knee, so the two knees sit closer together than the two hips. That slant is why the load line of the leg passes through the knee and not down the middle of the bone.

structures.name: right hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone
structures.narration: The upper end of the femur is captured in the acetabulum. Everything above the intertrochanteric line belongs to the Proximal femur scene; here the hip is only the anchor at the top of the bone.

structures.name: right patella
structures.label: Patella
structures.narration: The patella slides in the groove on the front of the lower end — the patellar surface. That groove has a higher lateral lip, which is the bony reason the patella does not simply slip sideways when the quadriceps pulls.

structures.name: right tibia
structures.label: Tibia
structures.narration: The two condyles at the lower end roll and glide on the tibial plateau. The medial condyle reaches further down than the lateral one, which is what levels the knee joint line even though the shaft comes in at a slant.

structures.name: right fibula
structures.label: Fibula
structures.narration: The fibula takes no part in the knee joint itself. Its head lies below and behind the lateral condyle, and the lateral collateral ligament runs from the epicondyle down to it.

structures.name: right vastus lateralis
structures.label: Vastus lateralis
structures.narration: Takes the lateral lip of the linea aspera and sweeps round the outside of the shaft. Notice how far up its origin runs — as high as the gluteal tuberosity.

structures.name: right vastus medialis
structures.label: Vastus medialis
structures.narration: Takes the medial lip of the same ridge and follows it up along the spiral line to the intertrochanteric line. Lateral lip and medial lip, one vastus each — that is the simplest way to hold the linea aspera in mind.

structures.name: right vastus intermedius
structures.label: Vastus intermedius
structures.narration: The only muscle that arises from the flat front and side of the shaft rather than from a ridge. In a cross section it is the muscle sitting directly on the bone.

structures.name: right adductor longus
structures.label: Adductor longus
structures.narration: Comes from the front of the pubis to the middle third of the linea aspera. The adductors reach the same ridge as the vasti but from the opposite side of the bone, so the linea aspera is where the front and the inside of the thigh meet.

structures.name: right adductor brevis
structures.label: Adductor brevis
structures.narration: A shorter fan to the pectineal line and the upper part of the linea aspera, lying behind pectineus and adductor longus.

structures.name: right adductor magnus
structures.label: Adductor magnus
structures.narration: The largest attachment on the whole bone. It runs almost the entire length of the back of the shaft, from the gluteal tuberosity down the linea aspera and the medial supracondylar line, and ends on the adductor tubercle. The gap between its lower fibres and the tubercle is the adductor hiatus, where the femoral vessels pass behind the bone to become popliteal.

structures.name: right pectineus
structures.label: Pectineus
structures.narration: Runs from the pecten pubis to the pectineal line of the femur, the short ridge from the lesser trochanter to the linea aspera. It makes part of the floor of the femoral triangle.

structures.name: short head of right biceps femoris
structures.label: Biceps femoris — short head
structures.narration: The only hamstring that starts on the femur rather than the ischial tuberosity — it arises from the linea aspera and the lateral supracondylar line. It is also the only one supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve. A muscle that begins on the shaft cannot extend the hip, which is why the short head flexes the knee only.

structures.name: right gluteus maximus
structures.label: Gluteus maximus
structures.narration: Only about a quarter of its fibres reach the bone; they land on the gluteal tuberosity, the rough upward continuation of the lateral lip of the linea aspera. The rest go into the iliotibial tract.

structures.name: right popliteus
structures.label: Popliteus
structures.narration: A small muscle arising from a pit on the outer side of the lateral condyle, inside the knee joint capsule. Its origin is on the femur but it pulls on the tibia, and it is the muscle that unlocks a fully extended knee before flexion can begin.

structures.name: medial head of right gastrocnemius
structures.label: Gastrocnemius — medial head
structures.narration: Starts above the medial condyle, on the popliteal surface. Because it comes off the femur, gastrocnemius crosses the knee as well as the ankle.

structures.name: lateral head of right gastrocnemius
structures.label: Gastrocnemius — lateral head
structures.narration: Starts on the back of the lateral condyle. The two heads and the two hamstrings above them box in the popliteal fossa, and the popliteal surface of the femur is its floor.

structures.name: right psoas major
structures.label: Psoas major
structures.narration: Ends on the lesser trochanter, the highest attachment on the medial side. Its pull is what flexes and externally rotates the upper fragment when the shaft breaks.

structures.name: right iliotibial tract
structures.label: Iliotibial tract
structures.narration: The fascia lata thickens laterally into this band and sends septa inwards to the linea aspera. Those septa are the walls between the three compartments of the thigh, and the ridge on the back of the femur is where all of them are anchored.

structures.label: Adductor tubercle
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT, the single point where adductor magnus meets the femur (gap 0.49 mm) on a 440 mm bone; tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA24474 --contact FMA22459. Re-measured at this audit and unchanged when the search is restricted to the distal 15% of the shaft (--slab z:0,0.15), which is the check that it is not being pulled up the linea aspera by the adductor part of the muscle. It lies 33 mm from the medial epicondyle and 25 mm above it, the relation this scene's beat 4 states in words.
structures.narration: The bony end of the medial supracondylar line, measured where the hamstring part of adductor magnus takes hold of the femur. Put a thumb on the medial epicondyle and slide it about two and a half centimetres up the medial supracondylar line and you are on it. The tendon running to it is the medial edge of the adductor hiatus, so this point marks where the femoral artery leaves the thigh and becomes popliteal.

structures.label: Medial epicondyle
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: EXTREME +x within the distal 15% of the bone — the most medial point of the lower end (+x is the body's left, so on this right femur it is the medial side); tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA24474 --extreme +x --slab z:0,0.15. Cross-checked against the adductor tubercle contact point, 33 mm away and 25 mm below it.
structures.narration: The bump you can feel on the inner side of the knee, above the joint line. The tibial collateral ligament takes off from it, and the adductor tubercle sits about two and a half centimetres above it — which is why the epicondyle is the landmark you find first and count up from.

views.title: One bone, hip to knee
views.narration: The femur spans the whole thigh. It is a ball joint at the top and a hinge at the bottom, and everything between is a tube of bone for muscles to pull on. Length matters clinically: measure from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial malleolus and you are testing whether the two femurs are the same.

views.title: The bone alone
views.narration: Strip everything off and look at the front. It is almost featureless — smooth shaft, the patellar groove at the bottom. Every rough marking on this bone is on the back, and that is not an accident: the muscles that need leverage pull backwards on it.

views.title: The linea aspera
views.narration: Turn it round. The vertical ridge down the middle of the back is the linea aspera, and it has a medial and a lateral lip. Trace it upwards and the lateral lip becomes the gluteal tuberosity while the medial lip becomes the spiral line to the intertrochanteric line. Trace it downwards and the two lips diverge into the supracondylar lines, enclosing the flat popliteal surface. Learn the ridge and you have learnt most of the bone.

views.title: The lower end
views.narration: From below, the lower end is two condyles separated behind by the intercondylar fossa and joined in front by the patellar surface. The medial condyle is longer, and the two lit points on its inner side are measured, not sketched: the medial epicondyle, and the adductor tubercle twenty-five millimetres above it at the end of the medial supracondylar line. The cruciate ligaments take their femoral attachments from the walls of that fossa — the anterior cruciate from the medial side of the lateral condyle, the posterior cruciate from the lateral side of the medial condyle.

views.title: Everything that pulls on the shaft
views.narration: Almost the entire back of the shaft is muscle attachment. The adductors come to it from the inside, the vasti from the front and side, gluteus maximus and the short head of biceps from above and behind. Adductor magnus alone covers the ridge from top to bottom.

views.title: A hollow tube, not a solid rod
views.narration: Slide the cut down the shaft. In the middle third the wall is thick compact bone around a wide medullary cavity — the shaft is a tube. A tube resists bending nearly as well as a solid rod of the same outer size but weighs far less, which is the whole design of a long bone. Move the cut towards either end and the cavity opens out into spongy cancellous bone with no true cavity at all.

views.title: What is inside the cavity
views.narration: The medullary cavity holds marrow — red and haemopoietic in a child, replaced by yellow fatty marrow in the adult shaft. It is lined by endosteum and the bone outside is covered by periosteum, and both layers are where new bone comes from after a fracture. That fatty marrow is also why a femoral shaft fracture can throw fat globules into the circulation and produce fat embolism syndrome a day or two later.

views.title: How the bone is fed
views.narration: The path traced here is the nutrient artery, a branch of a perforating artery from the profunda femoris. It enters through a nutrient foramen near the linea aspera, angled away from the growing end, and supplies the inner two thirds of the cortex. The outer third is fed from periosteal vessels. Strip the periosteum carelessly at surgery and you take away half the blood supply of the shaft.

views.title: The three compartments around it
views.narration: Cut across the mid-thigh and the femur sits slightly towards the back with three compartments arranged around it. Anterior holds the quadriceps and the femoral nerve, medial holds the adductors and the obturator nerve, posterior holds the hamstrings and the sciatic nerve. The septa that divide them all run from the fascia lata to the linea aspera, so the ridge on the bone is the hinge of the whole arrangement.

views.title: When the shaft breaks
views.narration: It takes great force to break this shaft, so assume other injuries. The muscles then deform the fragments in a predictable way: psoas and the gluteal muscles flex and rotate the upper fragment outwards, the adductors pull the lower fragment medially, and gastrocnemius tilts the very lowest fragment backwards towards the popliteal artery. A closed femoral shaft fracture can hide a litre or more of blood in the thigh, which is enough to make a young adult shocked with no external bleeding at all.

views.title: Peel down to bone
views.narration: Peel the thigh in order: fascia lata, then the muscles of each compartment, then periosteum, then cortex, then the cavity. Reciting that order is how you answer any question about the femur — it tells you what a surgeon passes through to reach the bone, and what a nail passes down once inside it.

gaps: The medullary cavity, the endosteum, the periosteum, the trabecular pattern and the epiphyseal plates are internal architecture that a surface model cannot show. The cut-plane beats open the outer shell and describe what a real sawn section would reveal; the marrow itself is authored as a traced concept rather than displayed.

The linea aspera, the gluteal tuberosity, the pectineal and spiral lines, the supracondylar lines, the intercondylar fossa, the nutrient foramen and the patellar surface are sub-features of one whole-femur mesh, taught by lighting the femur and naming the feature. Two of the features formerly on this list are no longer estimated: the adductor tubercle and the medial epicondyle are now measured anchors (contact with adductor magnus at 0.49 mm, and the most medial point of the distal 15% of the bone). The remaining features are ridges and lines rather than points, which is neither definition the landmark tool offers, so they stay narrated.

No artery of the lower limb below the external iliac exists in the catalog, so the nutrient artery, the profunda femoris and its perforating branches are authored as a traced concept path along the back of the shaft and named in narration.

No ligament of the knee exists in the catalog — the only ligaments in it are the inguinal and the long plantar. The cruciates, the collaterals and the knee capsule are named in the lower-end beat but not shown, so the femoral attachments of the cruciate ligaments are narration only.

The adductor hiatus is defined by the gap between adductor magnus and the femur rather than by a modelled opening, and the femoral vessels that pass through it have no models, so the hiatus is described at the measured adductor tubercle anchor where adductor magnus ends.

This scene does not cover Proximal femur, Hip joint or Quadriceps femoris. The upper end, the acetabulum and the four heads of quadriceps appear here only as the ends of the bone and the muscles hanging off the shaft; the retinacular blood supply of the head belongs to the Proximal femur scene and is deliberately not repeated.
